items.scenario: You need to fix a bug that spans a 400-file service. A teammate suggests copying the 'relevant' files into a chat window and asking Claude there.
items.question: Why is Claude Code the better surface for this task?
options: Chat runs a weaker model than Claude Code, so its code answers are worse
It searches the live repo, edits files in place and runs the tests itself
Claude Code doesn't count against usage limits, so long tasks cost less
Chat can't read source files at all, so the paste would simply be rejected
items.explanation: Repository work needs the real file state, targeted search and a verification loop. Pasting is partial, stale, and leaves verification to you.
distractors: The same model families are available in both; the difference is access to the repo and the ability to act.
Claude Code on a subscription counts against the same plan limits.
Chat accepts pasted code and uploads; the problem is partial, stale context and no way to run anything.

items.scenario: It's your first Claude Code session in a repository you've never seen. You have a ticket to change how discounts are calculated.
items.question: What should your first prompts be?
options: 'Implement the discount change from the ticket', then review whatever it produces
'Read every file in the repo first so you have full context before we start'
Questions only: what it does, where discounts live, how tests run; then a plan
Switch to bypassPermissions so exploring the repo isn't interrupted by prompts
items.explanation: Questions before changes build context and let you judge Claude's understanding at zero risk; a plan before edits lets you correct the approach cheaply.
distractors: Asking for changes first means you approve actions before you know whether it understood the code.
Reading everything floods the context window; agentic search fetches what's relevant.
Widest permission on an unfamiliar repo is exactly backwards.

items.scenario: You want Claude Code to propose a refactor of the payment module, but you don't want anything changed until you've agreed the approach with your tech lead.
items.question: Which permission mode fits?
options: plan: Claude explores and proposes, but makes no edits to your source
acceptEdits: file edits apply automatically while commands still ask
bypassPermissions: so nothing interrupts the analysis of the module
auto: the classifier lets through only edits it judges to be safe
items.explanation: Plan mode is for exploring and proposing: Claude reads files and can run exploratory commands, but doesn't edit your source. It is the right mode before any non-trivial change that needs agreement.
distractors: acceptEdits applies file changes without asking, the opposite of 'nothing changes yet'.
Bypass removes the approval gate and is never needed to produce a proposal.
Auto may still make edits it judges safe; you asked for none until the approach is agreed.

items.scenario: A colleague is annoyed by approval prompts on their laptop and plans to run Claude Code with bypassPermissions for all daily work.
items.question: What's the best advice?
options: Fine, as long as they always work on a feature branch and never directly on main
Fine, because /rewind checkpoints can undo anything that goes wrong in the session
No: add allow rules for safe commands or use auto; keep bypass for sandboxes/CI
Fine, as long as they run the most capable model at the highest effort level
items.explanation: On a laptop, bypass gives any wrong turn or injected instruction your SSH keys, cloud credentials, other repos and push rights. Reduce friction with rules, not by removing the boundary.
distractors: A branch protects the repo's history, not the rest of the machine (credentials, other directories, network).
Checkpoints cover Claude's file edits, not side effects of shell commands like deletions, pushes or network calls.
Model capability doesn't make unchecked execution safe; mistakes and injections still happen.

items.scenario: Claude Code tells you, confidently, that request validation for /orders happens in middleware/validate.ts and cites line 42.
items.question: What's the right habit before building on this answer?
options: Accept it; with full repository access, its file and line citations are reliable
Open the cited file and line, and check the tool trail shows it read that file
Ask the same question in a fresh session and accept it if both answers match
Ask Claude how confident it is and accept the answer if it says it is certain
items.explanation: Repo access reduces but doesn't eliminate errors. Verifying a cited file:line is cheap and is the competency the M6.1 exercises train.
distractors: Access to files doesn't guarantee it read the right one or interpreted it correctly.
Non-determinism means repeats can agree and still be wrong; consistency isn't verification.
Self-reported confidence isn't evidence; the code is.

items.scenario: You're about to let Claude Code attempt a risky change to the build configuration of a working repository.
items.question: What should you do first?
options: Nothing extra; /rewind can undo whatever the build change ends up doing
Create a branch and commit the working tree for a known-good point
Copy the entire repository to a backup folder outside the project first
Switch to acceptEdits so the whole change is applied in one atomic step
items.explanation: Branch first, commit early: Git gives a complete, reliable rollback independent of Claude Code's own checkpoints.
distractors: Checkpoints don't undo shell side effects, and relying on one mechanism is fragile.
Clumsy and easy to get out of sync; Git already gives cheap, precise rollback.
acceptEdits changes how approvals work, not whether you can roll back.

items.scenario: After two hours, one Claude Code session has fixed a CSS bug, investigated a DB timeout and reviewed a PR. Now you start an unrelated authentication task and answers seem muddled.
items.question: What's the most likely cause and fix?
options: The model is overloaded at this time of day; wait an hour and retry
Leftover context from the earlier tasks; /clear before the new task
The repo is too large for one session; split it into smaller repos
The session hit its usage limit; switch to a smaller, faster model
items.explanation: Everything in the session competes for attention in the context window. /clear between unrelated tasks; /compact to trim within one task.
distractors: Nothing suggests a service problem; the symptom matches accumulated irrelevant context.
Agentic search handles large repos; the issue is session hygiene, not repo size.
Hitting a usage limit stops work with a message; it doesn't muddle answers, and a smaller model won't clear polluted context.

items.scenario: Your team wants Claude Code to automatically fix lint errors on every pull request in CI.
items.question: Which setup is appropriate?
options: A developer laptop running bypassPermissions on a nightly schedule
An ephemeral CI container, scoped tokens, no prod secrets, results as a PR
A CI job holding production credentials so each fix is tested against live systems
Nowhere; Claude Code can't run unattended, so the fixes stay manual
items.explanation: Unattended runs need autonomy, so the boundary moves to the environment: a disposable, isolated container with minimal credentials. Bypass-level autonomy is acceptable there, and a human reviews the output as a PR.
distractors: A laptop is exactly where bypass is never appropriate, scheduled or not.
Production credentials in an autonomous run maximise blast radius.
Claude Code supports CI use (e.g. GitHub Actions); the question is how to sandbox it.

items.scenario: Your repository contains a .env file with real staging credentials. You want Claude Code to be able to run tests freely but never read secrets.
items.question: Which control is most reliable?
options: A line in CLAUDE.md telling Claude it must never open or print the .env file
Auto mode's classifier, which will recognise the file as sensitive
Deny rules such as Read(./.env*) in settings, plus an allow rule for tests
Renaming .env to config.txt so it no longer looks like a secrets file
items.explanation: Deny rules are deterministic, enforced by the harness before a tool runs, and apply in every permission mode. Instructions and classifiers are probabilistic; use rules for 'must never'. Better still, keep real secrets out of the working tree.
distractors: CLAUDE.md is guidance the model reads, not an enforced control.
The classifier is a judgement call — useful for grey areas, not guaranteed for must-never cases.
Obscurity doesn't protect secrets; it just hides them from you.

items.scenario: During a session, Claude ran a migration script that dropped a local test table and also edited three source files. You want to undo everything.
items.question: Which statement is accurate?
options: /rewind to the last checkpoint restores both the files and the dropped table
/rewind restores the file edits; rebuild the table by rerunning the seed
Nothing can be undone once a command has run, so restore from backups
git restore . brings back the edited files and the dropped table together
items.explanation: Checkpoints track Claude's file edits, not external effects of commands. Git manages file history only. External state needs its own recovery path, which is why risky commands deserve Manual approval.
distractors: Checkpoints don't capture database or other external state.
File edits are recoverable via /rewind or Git; only the external effect needs separate recovery.
Git tracks files in the repo, not database contents.
